title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- August 18, 2026 (Correction and Gap-Coverage Cycle)
headline: The last briefing reported zero score changes. Sixteen scores moved days later.
summary: Compassion Benchmark's last briefing, published August 11, told readers that no scores had changed that cycle. That was accurate at the time. Two days later, a backlog of already-reviewed findings was approved for release, and on August 16 sixteen scores moved on the live rankings. Six crossed from one performance band into another: Cerebras Systems, Microsoft AI, Baxter International and Taipei moved down from their top bands, while Uganda and Guinea-Bissau fell into the Critical band. A separate cleanup the next day found that the Fortune 500 list had counted one company twice, under two slightly different names; the duplicate was removed, cutting the list from 448 companies to 447, with no score change involved. Most of the sixteen moves were not new bad behavior. Ten were placeholder corrections -- companies and countries that had never been measured one by one, and instead shared one generic starting score with dozens of peers. Cerebras Systems is the clearest example: a dedicated review found zero evidence of wrongdoing in either direction. Its score fell because it discloses almost nothing about its own workforce, not because it did anything wrong. Tonight's own review covered the seven days since the last briefing and checked 20 organizations. It produced eight new findings and confirmed twelve scores unchanged. Three of the eight are the same kind of placeholder correction: MetLife, HP Inc. and Marriott International were all published at one identical, never-assessed starting score shared by 23 Fortune 500 companies. Five rest on a genuine, individual assessment: Home Depot, Latvia, Washington University in St. Louis, Tenet Healthcare and Lagos. Lagos is the most significant finding. It is the first case filed under a new rule that lets a small score movement cross a band line when the movement is real, even below the usual five-point filing threshold. Lagos's finding passed the benchmark's own evidence test. Findings for Latvia, HP Inc. and Marriott did not pass that test, and are published as findings that failed it rather than being dropped.

pipeline.queueHandling: Twenty organizations were reviewed using an evidence window covering the seven days since the last briefing. Eight new findings were filed: five cross a published band line, and three hold within their published band. Twelve scores were confirmed within the benchmark's five-point range. Lagos is the first finding filed under a rule that lets a real but small score movement carry a published score across a line between bands. The published score for every entity named tonight remains unchanged.

topSignals.title: Lagos Becomes the First City Scored Under a New Rule for Small Moves That Cross Score Lines
topSignals.whyItMatters: Lagos is the first case filed under a rule built for exactly this: a small score move that still crosses a published band line. The finding also passed the benchmark's own evidence test.
topSignals.description: The Lagos State Government cleared waterfront settlements, including the Makoko community, between December 2025 and February 2026. More than 3,000 homes, schools and clinics were destroyed. About 10,000 people were displaced. United Nations human rights experts publicly condemned the demolitions in February 2026; residents reported deaths during the clearances, including a newborn. A reviewer first flagged Lagos over a separate event: a protest dispersed with tear gas on August 5, 2026. That dispersal was carried out by federal police, not the city government, so it was not counted as Lagos's own conduct. The demolitions were. The movement is a small one -- 3.4 points, from 20.3 to 16.9 of 100 -- but it crosses the line between the Developing band and the Critical band. Under the benchmark's ordinary rule, a movement this small would not be reviewed for publication at all. A newer rule closes that gap: any movement that crosses a band line is reviewed, no matter its size. Lagos is the first case filed under it. The finding also passed the benchmark's own evidence test, which requires at least one source making a finding specific to the entity, not a general or regional one; a UN human rights office press release met that bar. The state also suspended the demolitions in February 2026 and agreed to work with UN agencies on housing solutions -- credited as a genuine, if late, response. Lagos's finding has been filed and recorded. Its published score has not changed.

evidence.quote: Nigeria: UN experts condemn continued demolitions of informal settlements in Lagos
evidence.claim: United Nations human rights experts publicly condemned the Lagos State demolition programme.
evidence.source: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

evidence.quote: MASS EVICTIONS DISPLACE THOUSANDS IN LAGOS
evidence.claim: About 10,000 people were displaced and more than 3,000 homes, schools and clinics destroyed.

topSignals.title: Three Companies Get Their First Real Score -- And It Looks Like a Downgrade, But It Isn't One
topSignals.whyItMatters: MetLife, HP Inc. and Marriott were never individually scored before tonight. Their lower numbers measure what had never been checked, not new misconduct -- though the movement does cross band lines.
topSignals.description: MetLife, HP Inc. and Marriott International were all published at the identical score of 60.9 out of 100, a generic starting number shared by 23 Fortune 500 companies that had never been measured one by one. Tonight, each was reviewed individually for the first time. MetLife's reading fell furthest, to 33.1, because the company publishes almost no data on how it handles insurance claims -- no approval rates, no denial rates, no complaint counts. Sixteen of forty measured areas landed at the lowest starting point simply because there was nothing to check, not because harm was found. MetLife did settle a $23 million pension class action with more than 6,000 retirees, one day before trial. HP Inc.'s reading fell to 42.5. Its programme for monitoring suppliers is unusually strong, including weekly labor-metric reporting, but the company discloses far less about its own planned reduction of 4,000 to 6,000 jobs, announced in November 2025. Marriott International's reading fell to 44.4, the smallest drop of the three and the strongest underlying record: more than 1.2 million staff trained on human-trafficking awareness since 2016. Its own San Francisco workers still needed a three-month strike to win new staffing protections, ratified by 99.8 percent of members. All three movements cross out of the Established band. None of the three findings passed the benchmark's evidence test for a band crossing, because the strongest evidence behind each is the shared placeholder score itself, not an outside finding naming the company specifically. All three are filed and recorded, not applied. Published scores are unchanged.

evidence.claim: MetLife settled a pension-calculation class action covering more than 6,000 retirees for $23 million, one day before trial.

evidence.quote: HP to cut about 6,000 jobs by 2028, ramps up AI efforts
evidence.claim: HP announced a workforce reduction of up to 6,000 employees by fiscal 2028 alongside an AI transformation programme.

topSignals.title: A Border Operation's Start Date and Headcount Were Both Wrong in the Original Report
topSignals.whyItMatters: Latvia's published score turned out to be a four-country placeholder. The border operation behind tonight's finding also had the wrong start date and headcount in the original report -- both corrected here.
topSignals.description: Latvia's published score of 62.5 out of 100 is identical, digit for digit, to the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovenia -- four neighboring countries sharing one never-measured placeholder. Tonight's review measured Latvia on its own record for the first time and found a genuine, sourced finding: a militarized border operation named Vilkatis, using drones, helicopters and troops, aimed at migration from Belarus. An earlier report said the operation started August 6, 2026, and had stopped 9,310 people at the border. Both figures were wrong. Latvia's own Ministry of Defence, Euronews and Bloomberg all confirm the operation began August 11, 2026, and the official count is 9,521. Both errors were corrected before scoring. Amnesty International documents that 2024 legal changes let border guards summarily return migrants in practice, and that Latvia opened criminal smuggling proceedings against two aid workers helping migrants at the border. A case challenging the pushback practice is pending before the European Court of Human Rights but has not yet been decided. Latvia's reading fell to 48.8, crossing out of the Established band and landing near Hungary (50.2) and above Poland (42.2) -- two countries facing similar pressures that have already been measured individually. The finding did not pass the benchmark's evidence test for a band crossing, because the strongest evidence is still the shared placeholder score, not a court or treaty-body ruling naming Latvia specifically. It is filed and recorded, not applied. Latvia's published score is unchanged.

evidence.quote: New Security Operation "WEREWOLF" Began in Latvia's Eastern Border Region
evidence.claim: Latvia launched a militarized eastern border operation on August 11, 2026, using drones, helicopters and aircraft.
Amnesty International documents that 2024 amendments granted Latvian border guards powers to prevent irregular entries, producing unlawful summary returns in practice.

topSignals.title: A Prior Finding Overstated Oracle's Layoffs by Nearly a Third -- the Correction Argues Against a Harsher Score
topSignals.whyItMatters: A prior finding said Oracle cut 30,000 jobs. Oracle's own filings put the number at 21,000 -- a correction that argues against a harsher score, not for one.
topSignals.description: An earlier review set part of Oracle's current score using a reported layoff figure of about 30,000 employees, roughly 18 percent of its workforce. Tonight's review checked that number against Oracle's own fiscal filings, which record 21,000 job cuts, about 13 percent of the workforce -- a gap of roughly 9,000 people between the number used to set the current score and the number the company itself reports. The correction was recorded even though it argues against, not for, a harsher score. A further reduction is separately planned before Oracle's fiscal second quarter starts on September 1, 2026, and will be measured once it happens. Oracle's score was confirmed essentially unchanged, at 15.0 of 100 against a published 14.7.

topSignals.title: Home Depot and a Major University Get Measured for the First Time
topSignals.whyItMatters: Home Depot and Washington University in St. Louis had never been individually scored before tonight. Both come in well below their old, generic starting numbers once real evidence is checked.
topSignals.description: Home Depot had never been individually reviewed by the benchmark; its published score traced back to the index's original build rather than any dated assessment. Tonight's review found the company went to a federal appeals court in November 2025 to expand its ability to restrict union insignia at work, and repeated a 2024 pricing violation in a new 2026 lawsuit. Real strengths offset the finding: about $739 million in bonuses paid to non-management staff, and a hardship fund that has supported employees since 1999. Home Depot's reading fell to 41.3 of 100 from a published 57.8, staying within the Functional band. Washington University in St. Louis was also measured individually for the first time. The federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission sued the university on August 12, 2026, alleging it eliminated an employee's job after she complained about race-based separation in a mandatory training -- an agency allegation, not a court ruling. The university also eliminated 316 filled staff positions and skipped merit raises for the current fiscal year. It moved the other way on student aid, spending about $33 million more since 2022 and holding next year's tuition increase to 4.5 percent. The university's reading fell to 41.9 of 100 from a published 50.8, also staying within the Functional band. Both findings are filed and recorded, not applied.

evidence.quote: National Labor Relations Act Protections for Union Insignia and the Evolving "Special Circumstances" Exception After Home Depot
evidence.claim: The Eighth Circuit decided Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. NLRB in November 2025, expanding the exception permitting employer restrictions on union insignia.

topSignals.title: Four Reviews Applied the Same Rule: Score the Government, Not the Harm Done Around It
topSignals.whyItMatters: Four separate reviews applied the same rule: score the government for what it did, not for harm caused by someone else -- a gang, a neighboring country's danger, or an ongoing conflict.
topSignals.description: Four unrelated reviews tonight turned on the same principle: a government is scored on its own actions, not on harm caused by someone else operating in or near it. In Thailand, officials raided a Karen village on August 10, 2026, and moved to deport 26 people to Myanmar; the danger those people would face in Myanmar is scored as Myanmar's doing, but every step of the raid, detention and proposed removal is Thailand's own conduct, and was scored as such. In Haiti, an armed gang attacked the town of Gros-Morne on August 7 and 8, 2026; the killings are not scored against the Haitian state, which does not control the area. Haiti's score held at 5.0 of 100, near the lowest point on the benchmark's scale, with little room left to move either way. In Lebanon, acute food insecurity affecting about 1.24 million people is driven by regional conflict, not by decisions of the Lebanese government, so only the government's own response was scored. In Zambia, the killing of a polling agent by an unidentified assailant was not scored against the state, but the state's vague new restrictions on civil-society groups were. Zambia's government also arrested nine people over the killing, credited as a responsive step. None of these four findings changed a published score by more than a few tenths of a point.

methodologyNotes.name: A Small Score Movement Can Still Cross a Published Band Line
methodologyNotes.description: The benchmark's ordinary filing rule reviews any movement of five points or more for publication. A separate rule requires filing whenever a movement crosses a line between two published bands, no matter how small the movement is. Lagos's finding this cycle -- a 3.4-point movement that crosses from the Developing band into the Critical band -- is the first case filed under this second rule. Without it, a real, sourced finding that happened to sit on the wrong side of a band line could go unreported indefinitely.

methodologyNotes.name: A Band-Crossing Finding Must Pass an Evidence Test Before It Is Filed, and the Result Is Published Either Way
methodologyNotes.description: When a proposed score crosses a published band line, the benchmark checks whether at least one independent, non-self-published source makes a finding specific to that entity, at a high enough tier. Lagos's finding passed, on a United Nations human-rights office finding naming the city government directly. Four other proposed crossings this cycle -- Latvia, HP Inc., Marriott International and MetLife -- did not pass, because the strongest evidence supporting each is a shared, never-measured placeholder score rather than an outside finding naming the entity by name. All four are published as failed tests, not suppressed or softened.

methodologyNotes.name: A Score That Has Never Been Individually Measured Is Not the Same as a Score That Has Gotten Worse
methodologyNotes.description: Dozens of entities across the benchmark's indexes were assigned one identical starting score when their index was first built, before any individual review took place. When one of those entities is finally reviewed on its own record, a large gap between the placeholder and the new reading measures what had never been checked, not new misconduct. MetLife, HP Inc. and Marriott International all fit this pattern this cycle, as have other entities in prior cycles.

methodologyNotes.name: A Government Is Scored on Its Own Conduct, Not on Harm Caused by Someone Else
methodologyNotes.description: When harm is documented inside a country or city's borders, the benchmark separates who caused it before scoring. A gang's violence, a neighboring country's danger to deportees, or harm caused by regional armed conflict is not scored against the government being reviewed; only that government's own actions and its own response are. Four reviews this cycle -- Thailand, Haiti, Lebanon and Zambia -- applied this rule.
